takeaway: FreePart isolates data-processing framework APIs by workflow phase, then tightens data and syscall permissions to contain framework exploits with modest overhead in tested applications.
background: Machine-learning and image-processing applications entrust large parts of their execution to frameworks such as OpenCV, PyTorch, Caffe, and TensorFlow. A memory bug in one framework API can otherwise reach the host application's code and data.
villain: General-purpose partitioning either needs difficult dependency analysis or incurs heavy copying, while isolating an entire framework leaves unrelated APIs and critical data inside one compromise domain.
approach: FreePart uses hybrid static and dynamic analysis to classify framework APIs as loading, processing, visualizing, or storing, then hooks calls so each class runs in a separate agent process. It tracks the current API phase to make earlier critical data read-only, applies seccomp-BPF syscall and file-descriptor restrictions, and uses RPC with lazy data copying between agents. Custom data structures require annotations, and security depends on correct classification plus a trusted OS kernel and FreePart runtime.
impact: The authors claim this framework-aware boundary can contain supported framework exploits without first deriving a complete code-level dependency partition.

evaluation.overview: The prototype was applied to 23 applications using OpenCV, Caffe, PyTorch, and TensorFlow, tested with application workloads and reproduced attacks from real CVEs.
evaluation.implemented: A 3,829-SLOC prototype used LLVM and PyCG for API analysis, C++ runtime support, inter-process RPC over shared-memory ring buffers, mprotect-based data permissions, and seccomp-BPF syscall filters.
evaluation.setting: Experiments ran on an Intel i7-9750H host with 32 GB RAM, Ubuntu 18.04, and a GeForce RTX 2060; workloads included application demos and tests, 144 GB of ImageNet-derived image/video data, and text inputs.

results.text: Across 23 programs, the authors reproduced eight attacks from 18 CVEs plus six case-study attacks and report that FreePart mitigated all of them, with no false negatives observed.
results.locator: Section 5, Correctness of FreePart; Table 5; Sections 5.3-5.4

results.text: The authors report 3.68% average runtime overhead across 23 programs, compared with 9.7% when lazy data copy was disabled.

limitations: The threat model covers malicious inputs exploiting supported framework vulnerabilities; host-application bugs, ML adversarial examples, a compromised OS, and compromise of the FreePart runtime are outside scope. Attackers retain control within a compromised agent process, and misclassified APIs or missing custom-data annotations can expose data or break functionality.
phd_group_signal: The work starts from an empirical workflow pattern, turns it into isolation boundaries and least-privilege policies, then validates both exploit containment and IPC-performance optimizations on real applications.

claims.text: FreePart partitions four framework API classes into separate processes, changes earlier data to read-only as the workflow advances, restricts each process's syscalls, and uses lazy data copy to avoid routing every object through the host process.

FreePart assumes an attacker exploits a data-processing framework through malicious input, while the OS kernel and FreePart runtime remain trusted; host-application vulnerabilities and attacks on ML algorithm robustness are outside scope.

A compromised agent remains vulnerable to attacks within that process, API miscategorization can grant access to sensitive data, and user-defined protected data structures require manual layout annotations.
claims.locator: Section 4.4.3 and Section 6, Impact of API Miscategorization and Impact of Intra-Process Attacks

claims.text: The 3,829-SLOC prototype was evaluated on 23 applications using an Intel i7-9750H host with 32 GB RAM, Ubuntu 18.04, and a GeForce RTX 2060, including workloads drawn from 144 GB of data.
claims.locator: Section 5, Implementation and Experimental Setup; Section 5.1, Program Selection and Workloads
